title: Mirabai
hook: a song signs its own name in the last line: Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and the song travels on

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai at a closed door in Vrindavan, answering that there was only one man there.

This week, three women's voices. Shakuntala, told twice, in an epic and in a play. Andal refusing a mortal groom, questioning a conch, dreaming her wedding. And Mira, dancing in bells and talking her way through a closed door. What reaches us of each one has been carried, retold, sung, by people who loved them. Mira's songs show it plainly, because they end with a signature. To close the week, the last line of a Mira song.
screen: `THREE WOMEN'S VOICES THIS WEEK.` → `CARRIED BY PEOPLE WHO LOVED THEM.` → `THE LAST LINE OF A SONG.`

segments.voice: Listen to how a Mira song ends. Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the clever one who lifted the mountain. The phrase comes back at the close of song after song sung in her name, like a seal pressed into wax. Singers call that kind of closing name a chhap, a stamp. It tells you whose song it is. Now, how do these songs reach us? By being sung: wandering singers, temple gatherings, women singing at home, families passing down the words they knew. And as they're sung, the same song can turn up in different words in different places. So when a song ends with Mira's stamp, what it promises is a voice and a lineage, not a notarized author. That raises an honest question the songs can't settle: which lines go back to Mira's own lips? Some readers sort the songs into older and newer. Others say the question misses the point, since a song stays alive by being sung, changing a little in every mouth. Both views take her seriously. Last, the stamp does something gentle. Whoever sings it, wherever, ends by stepping aside: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord. Each singer lends Mira their voice for a few minutes, and Mira lends them her love. That's how a woman who, tradition says, left a palace with almost nothing is still being sung.
screen: `MIRA'S LORD IS GIRIDHAR` · `THE CHHAP, A STAMP` · `CARRIED FROM MOUTH TO MOUTH` · `EACH SINGER LENDS MIRA A VOICE`

segments.voice: Bring back the three women one at a time: Shakuntala standing her ground, Andal with her conch and her dream, Mira with bells on her feet, and let each stay for a few breaths. Notice which voice stays with you longest, without deciding why, then rest in the breath. If you pray, you can give thanks for whoever carried their stories to you.
Mirabai. Her songs end with a stamp, Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and they've traveled from mouth to mouth, changing as they go.
Your line: Mirabai. Every singer of her songs ends on her name. I'll be here tomorrow.

chat.says: Why does every Mira song end with 'Mira's Lord is Giridhar'?
options: It's her chhap, a stamp: it marks the song as hers, and each singer steps aside for her.
It's a closing rule for all bhajans, so every poet's songs end on Mira's name.
It names the temple where the song must be sung, a temple called Giridhar.
chat.meaning: The closing name, a chhap, tells you whose song it is; whoever sings ends on Mira's Lord, not their own.
